analysis.one_liner: Requires beef sold in stores to be labeled with the country where it came from.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2025 and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it has sat without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring back mandatory country-of-origin labels for beef, so that grocery stores have to tell shoppers whether the beef they buy was born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States or abroad. A similar labeling requirement existed until Congress repealed it for beef in 2015 after a World Trade Organization ruling went against the US. Because of that history, the bill takes an unusual approach: it does not simply impose the labels, it orders the Office of the US Trade Representative and the Agriculture Department to figure out a version that complies with WTO rules and put it in place within a year. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who want to know whether the beef they buy was raised in the United States or abroad, and American cattle ranchers, who supporters argue could command a premium when US-raised beef is clearly labeled as such.

how_it_helps.text: Adds beef and ground beef to the list of foods covered by mandatory country-of-origin labeling, so retailers must tell shoppers where the beef they buy was born, raised, and slaughtered.
Requires USTR and USDA to find a way to reinstate the labels that survives World Trade Organization rules, in a nod to the earlier version of the law being struck down in a trade challenge.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers and beef importers, whose foreign-raised product would have to be labeled as such and might sell for less, plus retailers who would bear labeling costs.

drawbacks.text: A prior mandatory country-of-origin labeling law for beef was successfully challenged at the World Trade Organization and later repealed for beef, and the bill itself acknowledges this by requiring a new design that complies with WTO rules — meaning reinstatement may be difficult and could invite new trade disputes with beef-exporting countries.

The bill does not take effect immediately: labeling only starts once USTR and USDA implement a compliant approach, or one year after enactment at the earliest, so shoppers would not see origin labels right away.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Shoppers get clear information about where their beef comes at essentially no direct cost to consumers; the burden falls on retailers and on meatpackers and importers, whose foreign-sourced beef might sell for less once its origin is visible. The main honest caveat is that the earlier mandatory labeling rule was struck down after WTO challenges and cost US trading relationships; this bill tries to sidestep that by requiring a WTO-compliant design, but there is no guarantee one exists, which is why prior similar efforts stalled.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Agriculture Committee right after introducing it, and it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate on February 5, 2025, and read twice.
Referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which is where the record ends — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been taken.

The bill carries 11 cosponsors split between both parties, including Republicans Thune, Rounds, Lummis, and Hoeven alongside Democrats Booker, Heinrich, and Fetterman, indicating cross-party interest that has not translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shoppers have not gained the labels yet, and no interest group has lost anything either; the industry that would be labeled is currently better off because the requirement sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beef packers and importers so far

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Agriculture Committee.

for.name: Sens. Booker, Rounds, Heinrich, Lummis, Fetterman, and Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral; its record shows no hearings, markups, or votes on the bill to date.

sides.party_line_note: The 11 cosponsors split 7 Republicans and 4 Democrats, and the original cosponsor list itself paired 4 Republicans with 2 Democrats, so support crosses party lines.

industries.note: Labels revealing that beef was raised elsewhere could make imported beef harder to sell, and these companies have historically opposed country-of-origin labeling. Consumers could pay different prices if origin affects demand.
US-born beef would be clearly identified, which supporters say lets ranchers compete on origin rather than compete head-to-head with unlabeled imports.
Supermarkets and club stores bear the recordkeeping and labeling burden of tracking where each cut came from.
Consumers regain the right to see and choose based on where their beef was produced.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee with no hearings or markup scheduled. Country-of-origin labeling bills have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses and have not advanced; with no committee action after months, the likely path is that it dies in committee again unless leadership prioritizes it in a farm-related bill.
